- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are rising steadily, reduce forecast slope if true outcome shows early correction or mean reversion.
- If supply net is heavily negative (e.g., -10+ events/30d) and model forecasts remain flat or rising, adjust downward by 3–5% to account for bearish sentiment and supply shock.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >70), model often overcorrects; cap forecast rise to +2–3% per day after peak to avoid overshoot.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.67/0.00 alternation), model should not assume linear trend — apply smoothing or lagged decay to avoid overfitting.
- When official events are clustered (e.g., 3+ auctions in 5d), model should reduce forecast momentum — especially if supply net is negative — to reflect event-induced volatility.
- If true outcome deviates from forecast by >5% in first 3–5 days, adjust forecast downward by 1–2% per day to account for sentiment lag or policy-induced correction.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is weak (≤0.33) and price is trending up, reduce forecast slope to avoid overconfidence in bullish momentum.
- If model forecasts are rising while sentiment is bearish (≤0.33), apply downward bias of 1–2% per day to reflect sentiment override.
